1200.bp: Japanese companies and researchers need to search through financial documents written in Japanese—earnings reports, economic surveys, news—but the tools that measure how well these searches work have been built almost entirely around English. A good benchmark is what lets you know if a search tool is actually working.
1200.wh: Japanese financial writing has specific vocabulary, formality levels, and cultural context that English-focused benchmarks miss entirely. You can't just translate an English benchmark and expect it to catch the real problems that arise when a system tries to understand Japanese financial texts specifically.

The authors built the first benchmark designed from the ground up for Japanese financial text, including both retrieval tasks (finding the right documents) and classification tasks (labeling documents by sentiment or category). They tested many different models—Japanese-only models, multilingual models, and commercial services—to see how they actually perform.
1200.ww: A benchmark that reflects real financial scenarios forces models to handle both the general language challenges and the domain-specific terminology and context. By testing against multiple model types at once, you can see which approaches work best and where the gaps are.
1200.po: The benchmark is now public and gives the Japanese financial community a shared standard for measuring progress. This lets researchers compare their tools fairly and know exactly where improvements are needed.

1201.bp: When you search online today, you might want to find a research paper, the dataset it used, a survey variable it measured, or a tool that others mention—all from one search box. Modern search engines need to handle this mixed-category world, but existing evaluation benchmarks haven't caught up.
1201.wh: Most evaluation benchmarks assume you're searching one category at a time. Real users, though, want to find different kinds of things together: if I'm researching poverty, I might want papers, actual survey data, the specific variables researchers measured, and data-gathering tools all in one search.
1201.ap: The authors took queries from a real social science search platform and built a benchmark with four categories of results: Publications, Research Data, Variables, and Instruments & Tools. They used an LLM to write descriptions of the topics and to judge whether a result was actually relevant, which saved human labor.
1201.ww: When you evaluate a search system across multiple categories at once, you force it to rank items fairly across different types—not just finding the best paper, but also surfacing the dataset and tools alongside it. A shared benchmark makes everyone's systems comparable.
1201.po: The benchmark gives the research community a realistic testbed for building search systems that can handle the messiness of real scholarly information needs, where the answer is rarely just one type of thing.

1202.bp: News stories are full of events—a company's merger, a natural disaster, a political conflict—and extracting who did what to whom, in what order, across multiple articles is how we build timelines, understand causes, and prepare for similar situations. But large language models haven't been tested thoroughly on this kind of analysis.
1202.wh: Event analysis isn't just one task; it lives on a spectrum from the simplest (is this a merger event?) to the hardest (what's the causal chain of events across ten articles? what happens next?). Existing benchmarks test only pieces of this, and the data quality is often questionable because hand-labeling events is expensive and subjective.
1202.ap: The authors built a benchmark with four core tasks at increasing difficulty: detecting that an event happened, reasoning about how events relate to each other, inferring the full structure of a narrative, and predicting what comes next. They used an LLM-driven system to help generate labels automatically, then verified the quality, to make the process scalable.
1202.ww: By testing across all four levels, you expose which parts of event reasoning models actually understand and where they break. A good model might spot a merger event but fail to connect it causally to a competitor's response or predict the industry fallout.
1202.po: The benchmark shows exactly where today's best models fall short on real event analysis—whether in extracting details, cross-document reasoning, or forward prediction. This tells researchers what to build next.

1203.bp: Sometimes the answer to a question lives buried across multiple sources—you need to find the first source, then use information from it to know what to search for next, and repeat until you have the full story. Training agents to do this multi-step reasoning well requires examples of the right reasoning path.
1203.wh: Most training datasets show either the question and final answer (not the reasoning) or show multi-step reasoning but without the actual documents being searched. You need datasets that show what a good agent should actually *do*—which searches to run, in which order, and why.
1203.ap: The authors created a dataset of 9,000 multi-step questions (easy, medium, and hard) and had a state-of-the-art reasoning agent execute them, recording every search action and reasoning step. They then verified the final answers are correct. They also released open-source training code that lets you train agents using reinforcement learning with different reward signals.
1203.ww: When an agent learns from traces that show both the actions taken and the reasoning, it can imitate the patterns that work. Different reward signals—rule-based (did you find the right answer?) versus LLM feedback (does this reasoning step make sense?)—teach different things.
1203.po: Agents trained on this dataset and framework achieve state-of-the-art performance on challenging multi-hop reasoning benchmarks. The public release means anyone can build on it and try new training approaches.

1204.bp: As AI assistants become long-term companions in your life, they should remember your preferences, habits, and goals—not just answer the current question in isolation. But building and evaluating systems that actually do this well is hard because personalization happens across many subtle interactions.
1204.wh: Personalization has two hard parts: first, extracting what a user actually wants (some preferences are explicit, some hidden in how they respond); second, remembering and using that information correctly over weeks or months as conversations drift and preferences evolve. Most benchmarks either ignore this memory aspect or use fake, synthetic conversations that don't match real patterns.
1204.ap: The authors curated 2,500 long conversation sequences from WildChat (a real dataset of human-AI chats) and had humans mark down the explicit and implicit signals about each user's preferences. They then defined four tasks: can the model extract what it learns about a user, update that memory over time, retrieve the relevant memory when needed, and use it to give better responses?
1204.ww: Testing all four tasks in sequence reveals breakage at each step. A model might extract preferences well but fail to keep memories consistent as new conversations add information. Even if memory is perfect, using it to generate emotionally resonant responses is a different problem entirely.
1204.po: The benchmark shows that frontier models struggle most at memory updating and retrieval in large memory pools. Explicit memory structures help with recall but don't automatically make responses feel more personalized—pointing to new research directions.

1205.bp: Online marketplaces like Taobao face an endless stream of product listings that violate their policies—banned items, fake reviews, misleading claims. Using AI to catch these is critical, but vendors keep finding new ways to hide policy violations through word tricks, cropped images, or coded language.
1205.wh: Evasive content is deliberately designed to slip past filters while still communicating the forbidden claim. A model needs two rarely-combined skills: understanding complex policy rules and inferring intent from deliberately obfuscated text and images. Most benchmarks test one or the other, not both together.
1205.ap: The authors built a dataset of 2,833 Chinese text samples and 13,961 images from e-commerce, each labeled by experts with violation category and evidence of evasion. They tested 26 major LLMs and vision-language models to see which could both understand policy rules and catch intent-hiding tricks.
1205.ww: Obfuscation defeats simple pattern matching; the model must infer what the original forbidden product or claim was despite deliberate disguise. Evasive content forces reasoning about both rules and hidden intent simultaneously, which is where models typically fail.
1205.po: Even state-of-the-art models show significant gaps, especially on image-based evasion. The benchmark gives platforms concrete proof of what needs improving and gives researchers the data to build better defenses.

1206.bp: Climate scientists want to understand how communities experienced and survived past extreme weather—not just temperatures and rainfall, but how people responded, what broke, what held. Historical news archives hold these stories, but they're buried in millions of pages of old newspapers with poor image quality and archaic language.
1206.wh: Retrieving relevant historical news from a huge noisy archive is hard because old text recognition is poor and language changes over centuries. Then, even if you find the right documents, an LLM must pick out the human story—vulnerability, adaptation, resilience—from incomplete and sometimes contradictory 19th-century accounts.
1206.ap: The authors built a benchmark with over one million historical news segments. They designed two tasks: retrieval (find the relevant weather-related news) and assessment (can an LLM extract societal vulnerability and resilience indicators and answer questions about them?). They tested different retrieval strategies and different LLMs end-to-end.
1206.ww: Dense retrieval systems trained on modern text fail on old terminology and language patterns. LLMs often misread fragments of old narratives, filling in reasonable-sounding details that weren't actually there. Testing the full pipeline shows where each part breaks.
1206.po: The benchmark identifies specific failure modes—which retrieval methods struggle with archaic language and which LLMs hallucinate when historical text is vague—pointing researchers toward better historical understanding in AI.

1207.bp: Training trustworthy AI agents that can do complex reasoning requires them to show their work—not just the final answer but the step-by-step reasoning. Existing training data has a problem: it either shows only answers or shows reasoning that isn't grounded in actual documents.
1207.wh: To build an agent that searches documents and synthesizes answers, you need training data that shows real reasoning traces—which documents were examined, in what order, what each revealed. Without this grounding, an agent might learn to sound reasonable while making things up.
1207.ap: The authors built a platform called AgentSim that simulates what an agent searching through documents should do: it systematically explores a document collection, generates reasoning steps for each decision, and tracks what each step actually found. They used multiple LLMs to generate traces, had them debate when they disagreed, and used humans to verify hard cases. They released 103,000 reasoning steps grounded in real documents across three benchmarks.
1207.ww: When you train on traces where reasoning is actually tied to what the documents say, the agent learns the difference between sound reasoning and plausible-sounding nonsense. Disagreement between models reveals where reasoning is ambiguous, so human effort concentrates on the genuinely hard cases.
1207.po: The public corpus lets researchers compare how different models approach the same information-seeking task. It's concrete evidence that frontier models search differently and suggests new avenues for designing better agents.

1208.bp: User simulation is a way to evaluate search engines cheaply and automatically—you run a simulated user through a search system and see if it behaves like real users would. But today, building simulations requires coding expertise, which keeps most researchers from trying it.
1208.wh: Existing simulation tools are code libraries. They're powerful but require researchers to write custom code to design an experiment, run it, and share results reproducibly. This friction blocks adoption and makes it hard to share or repeat work.
1208.ap: The authors built a web-based workbench that lets researchers visually design simulation experiments without code, run them, and publish the results with full experiment details stored. The system tracks versions of components, makes it clear what was changed between runs, and supports sharing experiments through Git.
1208.ww: A visual interface lowers the barrier for novices to learn simulation concepts while still letting experts run large experiments efficiently. Version control and provenance tracking mean that anyone can verify whether results can be reproduced.
1208.po: The workbench is available as both a hosted service and a containerized version researchers can run locally. It demonstrates a real shared-task workflow, making user simulation more accessible to the IR community.

1209.bp: User simulators help evaluate search systems without recruiting real people, but simulators come in different flavors—some mimic human behavior closely, others produce reliable rankings of systems. These are actually different goals that can conflict.
1209.wh: A simulator that produces realistic user behavior might not produce valid system rankings, and vice versa. If you measure only 'realism' (does this simulator act like humans?), you might miss that it's useless for ranking systems. There's no standard toolkit for measuring both.
1209.ap: The authors released SimEval-IR, which measures simulator quality on two distinct dimensions with actual metrics. Behavioral realism uses metrics like click-depth distance and Fréchet distance of session patterns. Tester reliability measures whether a simulator correctly ranks one search system as better than another.
1209.ww: By separating measurement, you can see which simulators are realistic but don't rank systems properly, and which rank correctly but don't match human behavior. Different research questions need different trade-offs, so making the choice explicit matters.
1209.po: The toolkit and benchmarks show that the standard 'human-likeness' test used in prior work has almost no correlation with ranking validity. This finding redirects researchers away from a dead-end metric and toward metrics that actually predict system-ranking validity.

1210.bp: English-speaking researchers have many ways to build evaluation benchmarks for search systems using LLMs, but researchers working on Arabic face a problem: is this technique even reliable in Arabic? Do the same methods that work in English work for a different language?
1210.wh: LLMs were trained primarily on English text. When you ask them to judge relevance in another language, you don't know if they're applying the same logic or if language-specific quirks break their judgment. Existing studies all focus on English.
1210.ap: The authors took an Arabic test collection (ArTest), had three LLMs generate relevance labels for 10,000 queries and document pairs, and then checked: did the LLMs agree with each other, did they rank systems the same way as human-labeled data, and where did they differ?
1210.ww: If LLMs agreed with each other and with human labels, the method is likely reliable. If they disagreed, it points to language-specific problems—maybe cultural context, linguistic ambiguity, or LLM training gaps.
1210.po: LLMs generally work for Arabic relevance labeling, with agreement levels similar to English results. The finding is encouraging for researchers in languages with few labeled resources, though with some caveats around manually-verified high-performing systems.

1211.bp: A new retrieval method called the Hypencoder encodes search queries as tiny neural networks that predict which documents are relevant. The challenge is making this practical—spending less computation while keeping quality high.
1211.wh: Using a neural network as a query can be overkill for simple searches. You might be able to use a smaller, faster network without losing much accuracy. But adapting a system to use multiple sizes is non-trivial.
1211.ap: The authors extended the Hypencoder to support multiple query-network sizes, inspired by Matryoshka representation learning, which trains embeddings to work at multiple scales. The system can now choose a smaller network when quality loss is acceptable and a larger one when accuracy is critical.
1211.ww: Smaller networks have fewer parameters to compute during scoring, so they're faster. By training together, the smaller versions reuse insights from the larger ones, so they stay effective even with fewer parameters.
1211.po: In tests, the multi-size version achieves the same search quality with 7 times fewer active parameters in familiar data and half as many in new data, translating to 1.6-3.4 times faster throughput. This makes the Hypencoder practical to deploy.

1212.bp: When you search for an expert at a university or research institution, you might search by the person's name (looking for someone specific) or by topic (exploring who knows about a subject). Over a session, users often switch between these search modes as they learn more.
1212.wh: Most expert search systems treat name search and topic search as entirely separate problems. But real users mix them—maybe a name search yields a person who sparks interest in a topic, leading to topic searches, which lead back to looking for names. Understanding these transitions could improve recommendations.
1212.ap: The authors analyzed 500,000 queries submitted to an institutional expert search system, classifying each as name-based, topic-based, or unclear. They looked at whether queries in the same session stayed in one mode or switched, and whether clicks (signs of success) made mode-switching more likely.
1212.ww: Mode-switching happens, but more when a user finds something—a click prompts them to search differently. This suggests the system is working well enough that users feel confident exploring from a different angle.
1212.po: The finding that mode-switching is success-driven suggests expert search systems should explicitly support transitions—if someone finds an interesting person, offer topic searches about their work; if someone finds a topic area, offer names of leading researchers.

1213.bp: Online advertising relies on automatic bidding systems that allocate budgets across ad placements and adjust bids in real time. But these systems face a modern challenge: feedback is slow and noisy (it takes days to know if an ad led to a sale), making traditional control algorithms unreliable.
1213.wh: Sparse and delayed conversion signals (someone sees an ad today, buys three weeks later) break the feedback loops that control systems depend on. Traditional cost-per-acquisition targets become meaningless if you don't know which purchases came from which ads. Meanwhile, long-term patterns and advertiser intent are hard to encode into a control system.
1213.ap: The authors proposed a two-level system: an LLM analyzes ad content and historical trends to plan daily spending with explicit cost tolerance (high-level strategy), while a Model Predictive Controller tracks those plans via minute-by-minute bid adjustments (low-level execution). The LLM runs infrequently; the controller runs constantly.
1213.ww: Using an LLM to reason about high-level strategy lets you incorporate intent and patterns that a pure feedback loop misses. A controller then translates that plan into actions while staying robust to noise and delays.
1213.po: In production deployment, this system increased conversions by 1.8% and significantly improved stability when conversions are sparse. It shows how hybrid human-LLM-controller systems can handle real advertising complexity.

1214.bp: A recent retrieval approach encodes items as discrete IDs and treats search as generating the right ID sequence. To keep up with new items and changing popularity, these IDs need to be refreshed periodically, but rebuilding and retraining the whole system is slow.
1214.wh: If you create new IDs based on recent user interactions, the retriever—which was trained on old IDs—no longer works. Retraining from scratch wastes computation. The challenge is updating IDs without invalidating the existing trained model.
1214.ap: The authors proposed a lightweight update: given fresh IDs derived from recent logs, they align them to the old ID vocabulary so the trained retriever is still compatible. Standard fine-tuning then adapts the model to the new interactions without requiring a full rebuild.
1214.ww: By mapping new IDs to semantically similar old IDs, the model's learned patterns stay valid. Fine-tuning can then adjust for shifts in user behavior without starting from scratch.
1214.po: Across three benchmarks, this alignment update improves retrieval quality and reduces training compute by 8-9 times compared to full retraining. It makes it practical to keep generative retrieval systems fresh as items and user preferences change.
